# Extended Voyages

*Pages PDF 128-139*

## ## Extended Voyages
# **Extended Sojourns Upon the Sea and Trade Between Different Nations**
These rules are intended to allow you to resolve a journey of many days on a ship in a relatively short time in gameplay. As such, encounters can be generated and resolved quickly while facing the Players with tough choices. Of course, if the Players or GM are intrigued by an encounter, it can be expanded to become a more substantial part of the session, but the intent of these rules is to make sea travel seem dangerous and consequential without bogging down the narrative. 

Those finding things too dangerous would be well advised to seek the blessing of Manann’s priesthood, who can often smooth such troubles for the correct offering. 

Extended voyages are managed as follows: 

## **Very Quick Long Voyages**
It may be the case that, as a gaming group, the GM and Players do not want to spend time determining the details — even in broad strokes — of a particular voyage. If a GM only wants minimal engagement with the rules for a particular voyage, the following rules can be used to add a little flavour and drama to a swift resolution. 

   - Work out the distance of the voyage and the average speed of the ship (see next page) to determine the length of the voyage. 

   - Calculate Manann’s Mood and note the tens digit. 

   - Make a Hard Going Crew Test and record the SL. 

- The average speed of the ship is calculated and modified by prevailing winds to work out how far the ship travels in a day. 

- The GM should keep track of Manann’s Mood (see page 130). 

- Every d10 days at sea, a Shipboard Event takes place (see page 131). Manann’s Mood should be considered when generating an event. 

- If a ship docks at port, a Port Event takes place within 2d10 hours. Manann’s Mood has a moderate effect here. 

- For every full week of travel, a Shipboard Endeavour may be undertaken. 

For the purpose of determining events, days at sea need not be continuous. So, if the GM rolls 7 when determining how many days at sea pass before the next event and the ship spends 4 days at sea, then a week in port, the event occurs after a further 3 days at sea. 

- Roll on the table below, subtracting 1 for each week spent at sea and then adjusting by the tens digit from Manann’s Mood and the SL from the Hard Going Crew Test.

If any critical hits to the ship target crew, or risk causing injuries amongst the crew due to the Splinters Rating, ignore the damage done to members of the crew. 

Such losses are covered by the crew lost during the voyage and are not in addition to them. 

## **Average Speed of Ships on Long Voyages**
The rate at which ships travel is summarised in the following table. However, some factors such as load, weather, wind direction, and other calamities can alter a ship’s Move and thus change the distance it travels in a day. To determine how long a journey takes, a GM should first determine the distance to be travelled, then roll on the Shipboard Events Table (page 131) and resolve it. Then decrease the distance from the destination by the amount on the following table. Repeat this process until the ship reaches its destination.

## **Voyage Distances**
The table at the top of the page shows a matrix of voyage distances between major locations around the Sea of Claws. These distances are shown in miles and assume that vessels are at least 10 miles out to sea when they reach open waters, not hugging the coastline where rocks and wreckers could make journeys difficult. 

Distance covered per day assumes the vessel in question has sufficient crew and facilities to allow for sailing through the night. If this is not true, halve the distance travelled in a day. 

When using the Boat Handling Crew Test to make progress, any SL achieved can increase the day’s progress by about 10%. Negative SL will reduce it by a similar amount. These voyage times can also be helped and hindered, almost imperceptibly, by ocean currents. Poor weather does not add to these times directly but adds to the difficulty of pertinent Crew Tests. 

## **Events at Sea**
Those who travel at sea do so by the grace of Manann. Please him and it is likely that the voyage will be a smooth one. Incur his displeasure and the going will be rough. Manann is jealous and capricious, so even the most devout can’t be certain of his disposition. 

Each day at sea, review how the crew behaved towards Manann and keep a running total. You can only obtain each modifier once and sacrifices aren’t cumulative. This number applies to the ship itself, so it is possible for new crew to join a ship that has an existing modifier (for this reason, sailors are often reluctant to join the crew of a ship that has a reputation for displeasing Manann). 

On very rare occasions, a Character may incur Manann’s displeasure, or his blessing. In such cases, they may earn their own modifier to Shipboard Events, which would be added to (or subtracted from) the number for the ship on which they travel. As GM, you could apply modifiers based on other nautical superstitions — feel free to be as arbitrary and capricious as Manann! Just don’t ruin your players’ enjoyment. Manann may be temperamental, but he is not often sadistic. 

Every d10 days at sea the GM should roll on the events table to determine any unexpected occurrences. The rolls on this table are modified by the current number the ship has for Manann’s Mood, so a vessel that has incurred Manann’s displeasure is much more likely to encounter adverse conditions. 

## Other Powers of the Sea
When conditions become desperate, sea captains occasionally turn away from Manann and pray to darker powers to save their lives. If a shipbound character makes a pact with Stromfels, Mermedus, or one of the Ruinous Powers, they may be saved from a storm, monster, or sea battle. But rest assured, these darker powers expect payment eventually. It is also worth remembering that, whatever the worshippers of other powers of the sea may profess, Manann remains the preeminent god of the oceans. Other powers may be able to rescue their worshippers from Manann’s wrath, but it is only ever a temporary respite. Even the followers of Stromfels, whilst they hold contempt for Manannites in their hearts, are careful not to blaspheme against the sea god until they are back on dry land.

## **Events During Port Stays**
Arriving at port triggers a Port Event which is determined by the GM by rolling 2d10 and consulting the Port Stay Events Table (see page 133) as soon as the ship arrives. The event is determined when the GM deems it fit. Manann’s Mood is not so apparent when determining the outcome of Port Events: if it is negative, reduce the 2d10 result by 1, if it is positive, increase the result by 1.

## **Endeavours at Sea**
Every week (8 days) of travel at sea, each Character has the chance to perform an Endeavour. Because they occur at sea, these Endeavours are not subject to the _Money to Burn_ , _With Great Power,_ and _Elf Improvement_ rules ( **WFRP** , page 195). 

The following Endeavours can be taken providing suitable facilities and instructors are available: _Crafting, Invent, Training, Unusual Learning, Combat Training, Foment Dissent, Research Lore_ , and all Endeavours that involve training from **Up in Arms** . 

A successful _Foment Dissent_ Endeavour causes 2d10 Morale loss if directed against the officers of the ship. 

## **Opportune Trade**
Provided your journey takes you past convenient ports, you may attempt some opportune trade. A quick deal can accomplish much. You can invest up to the total free non-overloaded Encumbrance value of your ship in gold crowns. Make an **Extended Difficult (–10) Haggle** Test that requires 10 SL and allows up to three attempts. 

_**Example:** you have 200 Encumbrance free on your ship, you invest 200 gold crowns, then you make your 3 attempts and succeed. You gain 220 gold crowns._

## **Mapmaking**
You create a chart which can be reproduced and sold for profit but also provide records for navigation. Make a **Difficult (–10) Trade (Cartographer)** Test and name two ports. If you succeed, you produce a map which has a value in GC equal to the number of SL scored on the Test. While travelling between the two named ports, the map provides +2 SL to Navigation Tests. 

You may also attempt a free _Banking: Stashing_ Endeavour ( **WFRP** , page 196) when you craft the chart, hiding your loot in a location marked on your chart. Your stash is safe provided you keep the chart safe, but if anyone acquires your chart, the stash is discovered on a 50 or less rather than the normal 10 or less on the d100 roll. 

## **Train Crew**
Your crew could be a more skilled bunch. Choose one of your Skills that is relevant to operating a ship. You spend your time instructing the crew in this Skill. Make a **Hard (–20) Leadership** Test followed by a **Hard (–20)** Test in the Skill to be trained. If you succeed, increase the crew’s rating in the Skill you taught them by the number of SL scored on the Leadership Test and spend 2 silver shillings in expenses and celebratory grog per member of the crew trained.  You may not increase a Skill beyond your own advances. Only NPCs may gain advances from this Endeavour. 

**Example:** _A Character with 9 advances in Ranged (Blackpowder) could instruct a crew of 30. They score 5 SL on their Leadership Test, increasing the Ranged (Blackpowder) Skill of the crew by 5 advances and paying 60 silver shillings._ 

_If that Character carried out this Endeavour again with the same result, the crew's Ranged (Blackpowder) would increase to a maximum of 9 advances in total and again the Character would need to pay 60 silver shillings._ 

## **Ship Maintenance**
Wear and tear on a vessel is inevitable. Rotten planks must be replaced, new sail sewn, and barnacles scrubbed from the hull. This Endeavour is best carried out at port but can be done at sea at an additional –20 penalty; ports with extensive ship-building facilities provide a +20 bonus to the required Tests. When undertaking this Endeavour, make a **Challenging (+0) Trade (Boatbuilder or Carpenter)** Test. If you succeed, you spend your Ship’s Size in Encumbrance of Ship Parts and remove the effects of the Wear and Tear Shipboard Event. 

If your ship has lost Wounds, you may repair them at a cost of 2 Encumbrance of Ship Parts per 5 Wounds repaired. If your ship has any Critical Wounds, you may repair them by making a **Hard (–20) Trade (Boatbuilder or Carpenter)** Test. If you succeed, you spend your Ship’s Size in Encumbrance of Ship Parts and Timber and remove the Critical Wound. 

## **Maritime Trade**
Trade is the lifeblood of sailing. The colossal revenues it generates are all that can support the monstrous cost of running a vessel. It consists of two different enterprises: buying a cargo, and selling it. 

International trade does provide some additional benefits over local trade. Some ports reliably produce certain goods (termed Surplus) whilst others can be relied upon to buy them (termed Demand). Whilst sea travel presents many risks to merchants, the rewards can be rich indeed. 

## **Buying**
Purchasing a cargo is a three-step process. 

## **1: Type of Cargo**
First determine what cargos are available at a port by examining the Produces column and Surplus column of the Gazetteer. Ports with Subsistence listed in the Produces column do not produce cargos for sale. If the place has Trade listed in the Gazetteer, generate a cargo randomly from the Cargo table. This cargo is currently for sale in addition to any listed under Produces and Surplus. 

## **2: Size of Available Cargo**
Cargo size is measured in Encumbrance points. The amount of Encumbrance your ship can carry is determined by its Carries Characteristic. To determine how many Encumbrance points of a given cargo is available, add Settlement Size to Settlement Wealth to any Surplus of that cargo, and multiply the result by 1d10 x 10. 

If the d10 roll is a 1, this indicates that there is no cargo of that type currently available. 

_**Example:** To determine how much Timber is available in Salzenmund. The settlement has a Size of 3 and a Wealth of 4, so rolling a 4 on your 1d10 means that there is (7 times 40) 280 Encumbrance of Timber available for purchase._ 

_Luxuries (Silver) is a Surplus good in Salzenmund. With a Size of 3, a Wealth of 4, and Surplus Luxuries (Silver) of 1, rolling a 4 on your 1d10 means that there is (8 times 40) 320 Encumbrance of Luxuries (Silver) available in Salzenmund._ 

## **3: Haggling**
Multiply the Encumbrance of the cargo being purchased by its base price in the Cargo table to determine the total price. Then Characters may haggle with the vendor. Make an opposed Haggle Test with the merchant. This can raise or lower the price by 10%, or up to 20% if the Character has the _Dealmaker_ Talent. This procedure is described in detail in **WFRP** , page 291. 

The Haggle Skill of a random merchant will be 3d10+40. If the GM rolls two or more 10s whilst generating a merchant’s Haggle Skill, then that merchant possesses the _Dealmaker_ Talent as well. 

Characters may purchase less than the total cargo available, but any Haggle Tests made by the merchant seller benefit from +1 SL as they bemoan the hassle of splitting a cargo. 

Any Haggle Tests made to buy goods in the Surplus Column benefit from +1 SL, as local sellers are always able to offer good deals on such cargo. 

## Trade in Marienburg and Lothern
Marienburg is the greatest trading location in the Old World, whilst Lothern is the greatest trading location in the Elven Kingdoms. 

The Trade entry in the Produces column in these cities is representative of cosmopolitan markets. Roll three times rather than once to see what the random cargos are. Any duplicates indicate that the cargo counts as Surplus +1. 

The Haggle Skill of a random merchant in Marienburg or Lothern will be 3d10+55. If the GM rolls one or more 10s whilst generating a merchant’s Haggle Skill at these locations, then that merchant possesses the _Dealmaker_ Talent. 

## **Selling**
Once the cargo has been purchased, it may be transported to another port for sale. 

## **1: Find a Buyer**
To calculate the chance of finding a buyer, first you must determine what relationship the port you are attempting to sell at has to the goods you are offering. 

- If the port does not produce the cargo you have for sale, or if the port has Trade listed in the Produces column, there is a good chance of finding a buyer, particularly if there is a local Demand for the goods. 

Add the Size of the Settlement to any Demand for the cargo, then multiply that number by 10, adding +30 if the Settlement has Trade listed in the Produces column; this is the target number. Roll d100, and if the result is less than or equal to the target number, a buyer is found. Failure indicates that there is no interest in the size of cargo the Characters are trying to sell. If they wish, they may offer half the cargo instead — roll again against the target number. If this second attempt fails, there is simply no interested merchant. 

- If the port does produce the cargo you have for sale and does not have Trade listed in the Produces column, a potential buyer may still be convinced to take interest. 

International trade is a little more forgiving than river trading in that items from afar often benefit from novelty value even if they are equivalent to local goods. Provided the ship has sailed more than 100 miles, it can try to offload goods at a location which produces those goods. The seller must pass a **Difficult (–10) Gossip** Test. If they succeed, multiply the Size of the Settlement by 10 to find the target number. Roll d100, and if the result is less than or equal to the target number, a buyer is found. 

If you have not travelled more than 100 miles it is harder to sell the cargo; treat it as if you are selling to a port that produces a Surplus of that cargo. 

- If the port produces a Surplus of the cargo you have for sale, making a deal will be a challenge. 

It is very difficult to sell cargo to a place that produces it in bulk, even if you have travelled from distant lands. The seller must pass a **Very Hard (–30) Gossip** Test. If they succeed, multiply the Size of the Settlement by 5 to find the target number. Roll d100, and if the result is less than or equal to the target number, a buyer is found. 

## **2: Determine Offer Price**
If a buyer is found, they make an offer for the cargo based on the table below. This is called the Offer Price. 

||**Settlement**<br>**Wealth + Size +**<br>**Demand**<br>**Ofer Price**<br>1<br>–50% of Base Price<br>2<br>–25% of Base Price<br>3<br>–10% of Base Price<br>4<br>Base Price|
|---|---|

Characters may make an opposed Haggle Test against the buyer to increase the price (see **WFRP** , page 291). When both sides agree on a price, the sale is complete. If the Characters are unhappy with the price available, they are, of course, free to walk away from the sale. 

- If the port does not produce the cargo you have for sale, or if the port has Trade listed in the Produces column, there is a good chance of getting a good deal, particularly if there is a local Demand for the goods. 

Add +1 SL to the Haggle Test for the seller. If there is local Demand for a good, add a further +1 SL. 

- If the port does produce the cargo you have for sale and does not have Trade listed in the Produces column, buyers will drive a harder bargain. 

The seller suffers from –2 SL to any Haggle Tests they make. 

- If the port produces a Surplus of the cargo, sellers will practically have to pay buyers to take it off their hands. 

The seller suffers from –3 SL to any Haggle Tests they make. 

If the Characters have a cargo they simply can’t shift in a timely manner but which, for whatever reason, they want gone, there are always merchants on the lookout for desperate souls. Characters may always sell a cargo for a quarter of its base price at any Settlement with Trade listed in the Produces column or with a Demand for that particular good. 

## **Generating Available Cargoes**
When you need to generate a random cargo, simply roll a d100 and consult the table below. As some goods vary in availability throughout the year, use the row opposite the current season to determine the result. 

||**Spring**<br>**Summer**<br>**Autumn**<br>**Winter**<br>**Grain**<br>01-05<br>01-09<br>01-18<br>01-09<br>**Arms**<br>06-08<br>10-12<br>19-21<br>10-12<br>**Luxuries**<br>09-13<br>13-16<br>22-25<br>13-16<br>**Metal**<br>14-19<br>17-22<br>26-30<br>17-25<br>**Timber**<br>20-28<br>23-44<br>31-46<br>26-36<br>**Wine**<br>29-33<br>45-56<br>47-60<br>37-56<br>**Wool**<br>34-50<br>57-62<br>61-65<br>57-60<br>**Salt**<br>51-60<br>63-75<br>66-72<br>61-64<br>**Oil**<br>61-70<br>76-82<br>73-83<br>65-81<br>**Saltfsh**<br>71-90<br>83-90<br>84-90<br>82-90<br>**Ship Parts**<br>91-00<br>91-00<br>91-00<br>91-00|
